title: Commands, invitations, and the polite -e form
goal: Tell people what to do without sounding rude, make suggestions, forbid things, and use the one verb ending behind every polite request in Swahili.
bekal: the imperative: *soma!* for one person, *someni!* for several
the *-e* form: *nisome*, *tusome* — for suggestions, requests, and prohibitions

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Jikoni pamoja
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon in the kitchen at Amina's house. Her mother is making dinner and Budi offers to help.

lines.speaker: Mama:
lines.id: Budi, come into the kitchen! Sit here.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you, ma'am. Can I help?

lines.speaker: Mama:
lines.id: Yes! Take the knife and cut the onions.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Should I cut them small or big?

lines.speaker: Mama:
lines.text: Vidogo. Halafu weka ndani ya sufuria.
lines.id: Small. Then put them in the pot.
lines.literal: small-small. then put inside of pot.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Okay. What should I do now?

lines.speaker: Mama:
lines.id: Wait a moment. Don't put the salt in yet!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Sorry! I was in a hurry.

lines.speaker: Mama:
lines.text: Hakuna shida. Amina, njoo usaidie pia!
lines.id: No problem. Amina, come and help too!
lines.literal: there-is-no problem. Amina, come you-should-help too!

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Coming! Shall we start cooking the rice?

lines.speaker: Mama:
lines.id: Yes, go ahead, you two. And don't forget the coconut!

notes: **Swahili commands don't sound as rude as you might expect.** *Kaa!* (sit), *Njoo!* (come here), *Kula!* (eat) are said to guests as hospitality, not barked orders. What makes them polite is tone and small additions: *tafadhali* (please), *bwana*/*mama*/*dada* after them, or a smile.

**Naweza is a shortened ninaweza.** In fast speech, *nina-* often shrinks to *na-*: *nataka* (= *ninataka*), *nafikiri*, *naomba*, *nakuja*. These short forms are very common and fully correct; this book uses the long form so you can still see how it's built.

**Sufuria is a pot, and the other kitchen words are easy too**: *sahani* (plate), *bilauri* (glass), *kijiko* (spoon), *chumvi* (salt), *nazi* (coconut), *sukari* (sugar). *Nazi* here isn't a whole coconut but its milk — *tui la nazi*.

**Nina njaa literally means "I have hunger".** The same pattern works for other physical states: *nina kiu* (thirsty), *nina baridi* (cold), *nina joto* (hot), *nina usingizi* (sleepy), *nina haraka* (in a hurry), *nina wasiwasi* (worried).

**Vipande vidogo — doubling a word gives "small-small", i.e. in small pieces.** Swahili loves doubling: *polepole* (slowly), *harakaharaka* (hurriedly), *kidogokidogo* (little by little), *mbalimbali* (various).

grammars.title: Commands: one person and several
body: The command for one person is **the bare root** — drop the *ku-*, done. For more than one person, add **-ni** at the end, and a final *-a* turns into *-e*.
after: The four irregular verbs — *njoo*, *nenda*, *lete*, and *kuwa* → *uwe* — are the only ones to memorize. You'll hear them dozens of times a day, so they'll stick on their own.
Verbs borrowed from Arabic don't change their ending even in the plural: *fikiri!* → *fikirini!*, *jibu!* → *jibuni!*, *rudi!* → *rudini!*, *samehe!* → *sameheni!*
⚠️ Watch out: *kata!* means **cut!** (from *kukata*). A "word" is *neno*, plural *maneno*.

grammars.title: The -e form: suggestions, requests, and prohibitions
body: Swahili has one verb form that covers "so that", "let's", "please", and "don't" all at once. Its shape: **subject prefix + root ending in -e**, with no tense slot at all.
after: **Invitations** use *tu-*: *Twende!* (let's go), *Tuende sokoni* (let's go to the market), *Tule!* (let's eat), *Tuanze* (let's start). It's the form you'll hear most from any group about to head off somewhere.

**Prohibitions** slip in *-si-*: *usiende* (don't go), *usisahau* (don't forget), *usijali* (don't worry), *usiwe na wasiwasi* (don't be anxious), *msichelewe* (don't be late, you all). This is the only way to say "don't" — a plain command can't be made negative.

**Polite requests** almost always start with *naomba* (I ask) or *tafadhali*: *Naomba usaidie* (please help me), *Naomba maji* (may I have some water), *Tafadhali urudie* (please repeat). And after *lazima* (must), the *-e* form is required: *Lazima uende sasa* (you have to go now), *Lazima tuondoke* (we have to leave).

sections.title: Maagizo ya kila siku — commands you'll hear

blocks.text: *Nisaidie* already contains "me" — the insert *-ni-*, meaning "me as the target". That part is taken apart fully in the next unit; for now learn it whole, because it's one of the most useful sentences in this book.

On a daladala or bodaboda, these two commands are the ones you'll need most: *Shusha hapa!* (drop me here) and *Simama pale!* (stop over there). And at the market: *Punguza bei* (lower the price) — which you already used in unit 7 without knowing it was a command.
Swahili expresses most physical states and feelings with *kuwa na* — "to have" — just like French and Arabic, and unlike English, which uses adjectives.
The negative uses the *sina* you've had since unit 2: *Sina njaa* (I'm not hungry), *Sina wasiwasi* (I'm not worried). And for others: *Ana njaa*, *Wana kiu*, *Hana haraka*.

Two of these come from Arabic: *hakika* (certainty, from *ḥaqīqa*) and *furaha* (joy, from *faraḥ*). If you want to answer "how are you" honestly and with life, *Nina furaha leo!* makes far more of an impression than an automatic *nzuri*.

exercises.prompt: Make a command for one person, then for several.
Fill in the blanks with the right -e form.
items: Lazima u____ sasa. (kwenda — you have to go)
Lazima tu____ mapema. (kuondoka — we have to leave)
